content_list.content_text: The first critics and commentators to take popular cinema seriously tended to value the so-called "golden age" of the Hollywood studios in the 1930s and 1940s, somewhat arbitrarily labeling 1939 as "the greatest year in film." This orthodoxy was set aside by the argument that the 1970s were the best years of American cinema - although a simplistic version holds that the industry's domination by important and revolutionary works ended with the rise of the popcorn blockbusters of Steven Spielberg (b. 1946) and George Lucas (b. 1944).

information.contentTitle: Scenes from One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest
information.contentText: Actor Kirk Douglas, who had played the role of McMurphy in a 1963-1964 stage adaptation of Ken Kesey's novel, bought the film rights to the story and spent a decade trying to bring it to the screen, but could not find a studio willing to produce the film. He later passed the rights on to his son Michael Douglas, who would manage to produce the film in the '70s. However, Douglas himself, by then almost 60 years old, was considered too old for the role of McMurphy, which ended up going to Jack Nicholson, then 38. Douglas brought in Saul Zaentz as the film's co-producer.

content_list.content_text: At the start of the decade, a protagonist would likely be as complex as Robert Eroica Dupea (Jack Nicholson) in Five Easy Pieces (1970). By the end, he would be more two-dimensional, like Clark Kent (Christopher Reeve) in Superman (1978).

But it is worth remembering that, even before Spielberg's Jaws (1975) and Lucas's Star Wars (1977), the major studios were happy to ride any profitable wave. Critical hits and award winners such as The French Connection (1971), by William Friedkin (b. 1935), and The Sting (1973), by George Roy Hill (1921-2002), inspired films in which tough cops took part in car chases and nostalgic comedy-dramas about male friendship.

information.contentText: Some critics expressed concern about the presence of the young Jodie Foster during the shootout scene. However, Foster explained that she was present while the special effects used in the scene were being set up; the whole process was explained and demonstrated to her, step by step. Rather than being traumatized or upset, Foster said she was "fascinated" and "entertained" by the behind-the-scenes preparation for the scene. In addition, before landing the role, Foster was subjected to psychological tests to ensure that the role would not affect her emotionally, in accordance with California labor laws.

content_list.content_text: Freebie and the Bean (1974) combined the two formulas and was part of a wave of mismatched cop pairs in film and television (Black/white, man/woman, gay/straight, human/alien) that would continue through the 1980s and beyond. Paper Moon (1973) offered another mismatched pair, the smart-aleck orphan (Tatum O'Neal) and the con man who becomes a father figure (Ryan O'Neal).

content_list.title: Martin Scorsese's Classic
content_list.description:
"Someday a real rain will come and wash all this scum off the streets". So mutters tormented cab driver Travis Bickle, played with almost furious intensity by Robert De Niro, in the first of his acclaimed leading roles in Martin Scorsese's films. Bickle's job, crisscrossing New York from one end to the other ("anytime, anywhere"), gives him a sleepless view of the city's underbelly, everything that happens in the dark alleys that most people never witness. He ends up so accustomed to the world around him, however, that he feels numb, invisible and, ultimately, powerless.

Taxi Driver's portraits of urban disorder and malaise are as dark and claustrophobic as they come. The film has some elements of film noir (Bickle's voice-over narration, the jazzy score by Bernard Herrmann (1911-1975)) but departs radically from the pattern when it comes to storytelling. Taxi Driver unfolds like a noir told from the perspective of an anonymous stranger standing in front of a murder scene, peering over the police cordon to see the covered body in the street. What is this person thinking? How would they react when confronted with such vivid exposure to violence?

Scorsese, Schrader and De Niro seem to be asking viewers the same thing. Throughout the film, we are forced to observe the city from Bickle's relentlessly isolated perspective, with only a few glimmers of hope carrying us outside his maladjusted mind. He is Dostoevsky's "underground man", who emerges with a gun and a death wish, an antihero who takes justice into his own hands, taking a hands-on approach to cleaning up the city. "Here is a man who won't take it anymore," he announces triumphantly. "A man who stood up against the scum, the sluts, the dogs, the filth, the shit. Here is a man who stood up."

Is this what we want? In an ironic plot twist (of the "the end justifies the means" kind), Bickle ends up hailed as a hero in his own crusade, and it is hard to say whether Bickle's inadvertent triumph is not, in reality, a tragedy. Because the film has so skillfully knocked our moral compass off its axis, we are left struggling desperately in search of impossible answers.
content_list.credits: Summary based on the text by Joshua Klein, published in the book 1001 Movies You Must See Before You Die

content_list.content_text: Young audiences responded well to the anarchic antics of Donald Sutherland and Elliott Gould in M*A*S*H (1970), by Robert Altman (1925-2006), and to the unusual romantic pairing of Bud Cort and Ruth Gordon in Harold and Maude (1971), by Hal Ashby (1979-1989), as well as to the award-winning performance of Jack Nicholson (b. 1937), who won an Oscar for McMurphy in One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest (1975).

information.contentText: Sylvester Stallone wrote the screenplay for Rocky in three and a half days, shortly after watching the championship bout between Muhammad Ali and Chuck Wepner, held at the Richfield Coliseum in Richfield, Ohio, on March 24, 1975, with few expecting Wepner to win the fight. Despite the fact that the fight motivated Stallone to start working on Rocky, he subsequently denied that Wepner provided any inspiration for the screenplay.

content_list.content_text: More conservative audiences showed the same enthusiasm for old-fashioned heroes, such as tough cop Harry Callahan (Clint Eastwood) in Dirty Harry (1971), Sheriff Buford Pusser (Joe Don Baker) in Walking Tall (1973), and vigilante Paul Kersey (Charles Bronson) in Death Wish (1974).

content_list.content_text: The divisions in society examined from various angles in these films resonated in a series of productions about the cultural conflict in the United States, exacerbated by divergent opinions about the Vietnam War. The paranoid Vietnam veteran Travis Bickle (Robert De Niro) in Taxi Driver (1976), by Martin Scorsese (b. 1942), who fails as a political assassin and ends up as a vigilante hailed as a hero, represents one view of the war.

information.contentText: Woody Allen hated his work on this production. He thought it was so bad that he offered to direct a film for free if United Artists, the film's US distributor, did not release Manhattan.

content_list.content_text: Bonnie and Clyde (1967), The Graduate (1967), Night of the Living Dead (1968), Easy Rider (1969), The Wild Bunch (1969), and Medium Cool (1969) were made at the end of the 1960s, but it was in the following decade that their artistic and commercial lessons were put into practice.

The enormous flowering of creativity may simply be due to the fact that audiences turned into hits films that middle-aged or geriatric studio heads could not understand, and so they greenlit projects that baffled them, imagining that perhaps audiences wanted something as surprising as the bone that turns into a spaceship in 2001: A Space Odyssey (1968) or David Hemmings making photographic enlargements in Blow-Up (1966).

information.contentTitle: Scenes from Willy Wonka & the Chocolate Factory
information.contentText: Filming took place in Munich in 1970, and the film was released by Paramount Pictures on June 30, 1971. With a budget of just 3 million dollars, the production received positive reviews but did not achieve the expected commercial success, grossing around 4 million dollars by the end of its run. Decades after its original release, the film became a cult classic, mainly due to its repeated television broadcasts.

content_list.content_text: This gave rise to many films that came to be considered classics: not only films that flopped on release but later became cult masterpieces, such as Two-Lane Blacktop (1971) or Willy Wonka & the Chocolate Factory (1971), but also immediate hits and Oscar winners. Making The Godfather (1972) in the 1970s was not a particularly radical decision, since gangster films had been part of Hollywood's repertoire since the 1930s. However, entrusting the project to an inexperienced director whose last studio job had been Finian's Rainbow (1968), just because he was Italian-American, was a decision born of inspired desperation.

One complaint heard from the upper echelons of US politics and the armed forces after the defeat in Vietnam was that - leaving aside The Green Berets (1968) - Hollywood had let them down by not mobilizing the propaganda machine the way it had during World War II. Instead of Yankee Doodle Dandy (1942), young people went to see Woodstock (1970). Instead of Betty Grable showing her legs and the Duke taking Iwo Jima, Jane Fonda supported the enemy and Donald Sutherland looked stoned.

information.contentText: Principal photography began on May 19, 1976, on Long Island's South Fork, and continued periodically over the next ten months. Allen described the result, which marked his first collaboration with cinematographer Gordon Willis, as "a major turning point," in that, unlike the farces and comedies that had been his work until then, it introduced a new level of seriousness. Scholars have noted the contrast between the New York City and Los Angeles settings, the stereotyping of gender differences in sexuality, the presentation of Jewish identity, and the elements of psychoanalysis and modernism.

content_list.content_text: The best that cinema could do for the war effort was Patton (1970), by Franklin J. Schaffner (1920-1989), which could be seen either as a celebration of a great American military hero or as a subversive portrait of an Establishment figure presented as a dangerous lunatic, depending on the viewer's political stance (it was Richard Nixon's favorite film, to the dismay of its makers). There were even films, such as Alice's Restaurant (1969) and Big Wednesday (1978), in which the heroes had dodged the draft and the American military was portrayed, at best, as clowns and, at worst, as forces of evil.

quote.author: Sylvester Stallone

content_list.content_text: In its early days, Hollywood had been run by immigrant moguls who felt a desperate need to display their patriotism, to the point of supporting President Franklin Roosevelt, whose policies they personally loathed and feared. They were so caught up in what was happening in Europe that they made World War II a personal matter, to the point that films made between 1942 and 1946 seem more pro-government than the genuine propaganda films funded by the government itself.

information.contentText: The film is based on a novel by Loren Singer. While the novel followed witnesses to the assassination of John F. Kennedy who were killed, the screenplay changed the victim to a fictional politician closely resembling Robert F. Kennedy.

content_list.content_text: In the 1970s, the major Hollywood studios backed The Parallax View (1974) and All the President's Men (1976), paranoid visions of a government conspiracy. When Hollywood began making films about Vietnam, few would have pleased John Wayne: starting with Coming Home (1978), The Deer Hunter (1978), and Apocalypse Now (1979).

Perhaps the most important American filmmaker of the decade was a man who directed almost all of his films before 1971 (afterward, he mostly made quick, opportunistic productions): Roger Corman (b. 1926). While the studios were still trying to follow in the footsteps of The Sound of Music (1965), Corman was employing Francis Ford Coppola (b. 1939), Peter Bogdanovich (b. 1939), Martin Scorsese, Robert Towne (b. 1934), Jonathan Demme (b. 1944), Joe Dante (b. 1946), Robert De Niro, Jack Nicholson, Monte Hellman (b. 1932), and Paul Bartel (1938-2000).

information.contentText: The opening monologue, delivered by George C. Scott as General Patton with an enormous American flag behind him, remains an iconic and frequently quoted image in cinema.

content_list.content_text: Without Corman's approach - keep the camera moving, include nudity, season the clichés with humor, use music that isn't fashionable yet (i.e., cheap) but is about to be, and make sure there's a crumb of social commentary for the college kids - there would be no films like American Graffiti (1973), Mean Streets (1973), The Conversation (1974), Chinatown (1974), or Shampoo (1975).

content_list.title: One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest
content_list.description:
A project that actor Kirk Douglas (1916-2020) had wanted to make for years (he owned the rights, but by the time the film finally went into production, he felt he was too old to star in it), One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest earned his son, Michael Douglas (b. 1944), his first Oscar, not as an actor but as a producer.

Based on the bestseller by Ken Kesey, written after his experience working at a veterans' hospital in California, the film is set in a state mental institution where the wily nonconformist Randle P. McMurphy (Jack Nicholson) is committed for rehabilitation. Inside the institution, he is kept under the watchful eye of the sadistic Nurse Ratched (Louise Fletcher, in a role turned down by several major Hollywood actresses, including Jane Fonda, Anne Bancroft, Ellen Burstyn, and Faye Dunaway), and he soon stages a rebellion against her with the help of other patients.

A groundbreaking film that Kesey reportedly never wanted to see (he was supposedly irritated that the story was not told from the point of view of Chief Bromden (Will Sampson), as in his book), One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest became part of Oscar history when it became only the second film up to that time to win all five major awards. Each one was deserved: Czech director Milos Forman (1932-2018) created a hypnotic, humanistic film full of eccentric characters (among the actors who made their film debuts are Brad Dourif (b. 1950) and Christopher Lloyd (b. 1938)), and drew one of the best performances of Fletcher's career. Nicholson, naturally, is captivating as McMurphy, imprisoned yet witty and full of life, and the scenes in which he faces off with the despicable Nurse Ratched are the most electrifying in this modern classic of American cinema.
content_list.credits: Summary based on the text by Joanna Berry, published in the book 1001 Movies You Must See Before You Die

content_list.content_text: Corman's business plan also impressed other independents who were making films far from studio interference. Drive-ins and college cinemas in the 1970s were full of oddities and films that embraced a multitude of genres. There were action films with Black casts, softcore / hardcore porn, and road movies. John Carpenter (b. 1948) created a few films, and Clint Eastwood (b. 1930) went from star to star director. Terrence Malick crafted experimental, symbolic narratives such as Days of Heaven (1978).

information.contentTitle: Trailer for The Man Who Fell to Earth
information.contentText: The Man Who Fell to Earth retains a cult following for its use of surreal imagery and for Bowie's first film role, as the alien Thomas Jerome Newton. It is considered an important work of science fiction cinema and one of the best films of Roeg's career.

content_list.content_text: It was also the era of the "early, funny" films of Woody Allen (b. 1935), which led to Annie Hall (1977) - the moment he decided that just being funny was not enough - and the romantic comedy and declaration of love for New York, Manhattan (1979). There was still room for an intense, emotional drama like Kramer vs. Kramer (1979) - which won five Academy Awards.

From a group of young filmmakers came the summer blockbuster - Jaws. The film had its antecedents: at first, Hollywood saw Spielberg's film simply as a follow-up to disaster movies such as The Poseidon Adventure (1972) or The Towering Inferno (1974). It was only when Jaws became as successful as The Godfather that people realized how significant the film was, and from then on it came to be considered a "high-end" horror film.

information.contentText: Kramer vs. Kramer reflected a cultural shift that took place during the 1970s, when ideas about motherhood and fatherhood were changing. The film was widely praised for the way it gave equal weight and importance to Joanna's and Ted's points of view.

content_list.content_text: Another significant and influential attempt in this area came with Westworld (1973). From then on, studio resources were directed toward directors such as Spielberg, Lucas, Brian De Palma (b. 1940), John Milius (b. 1944), John Landis (b. 1950), and even their Italian godfather, Francis Ford Coppola. It is argued that Star Wars ended the wave of creativity with a shortcut to a childishness that was easy to exploit commercially, but Lucas wanted to create a sense of wonder, just like Nicolas Roeg (b. 1928) in The Man Who Fell to Earth (1976) or Close Encounters of the Third Kind (1977). Star Wars is even attuned to the politics of its era: its heroes are scruffy rebels fighting against an established order, and Grand Moff Tarkin and Darth Vader could represent President Nixon and his lieutenant Calley.

content_list.content_text: In the long run, it may be that the effects of Star Wars brought an end to the opportunities that benefited Hollywood in the 1970s. From Jaws to Star Wars - as well as in the films of John Carpenter, Walter Hill (b. 1942), and others - came a sense of rediscovery of the Hollywood classics, which led American filmmakers to draw inspiration as much from Alfred Hitchcock (1899-1980), Howard Hawks (1896-1977), and John Ford (1894-1973) as from Jean-Luc Godard (b. 1930), Michelangelo Antonioni (1912-2007), and Ingmar Bergman (1918-2007).

information.contentText: Days of Heaven was shot in Alberta, Canada, in the second half of 1976 with a budget of three million dollars and little planning. Malick and cinematographer Néstor Almendros relied almost entirely on natural light and decided on the day what would be filmed, infuriating some crew members who were not used to working that way. Malick's directing style also displeased the cast and crew, with him being described as distant and insecure. The shoot ran so far behind schedule that Almendros had to leave and was replaced by Haskell Wexler. In addition, Malick took three years to edit the film, struggling to find a rhythm and choose scenes. This was eventually solved when narration by Manz's character was added.

content_list.content_text: The boxing film about a hero who comes from nowhere can also be seen from this angle, although Rocky (1976) is far more interesting than its many sequels. It brought energy and a sense of fun back to a cinema that had run the risk of producing an excess of slow, sad films, and it drew a huge audience that had largely stayed away from productions that would later be considered important.
content_list.content_credits: Summary based on the text by Kim Newman, published in the book "Cinema: The Whole Story" by Philip Kemp

movies.title: One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest
movies.original_title: One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest
movies.overview: While serving time for insanity at a state mental hospital, implacable rabble-rouser, Randle Patrick McMurphy, inspires his fellow patients to rebel against the authoritarian rule of head nurse, Mildred Ratched.

movies.title: Taxi Driver
movies.overview: A mentally unstable Vietnam War veteran works as a night-time taxi driver in New York City where the perceived decadence and sleaze feed his urge for violent action, attempting to save a preadolescent prostitute in the process.

movies.title: Rocky
movies.overview: When world heavyweight boxing champion, Apollo Creed wants to give an unknown fighter a shot at the title as a publicity stunt, his handlers choose palooka Rocky Balboa, an uneducated collector for a Philadelphia loan shark. Rocky teams up with trainer  Mickey Goldmill to make the most of this once in a lifetime break.

movies.title: Kramer vs. Kramer
movies.overview: Ted Kramer is a career man for whom his work comes before his family. His wife Joanna cannot take this anymore, so she decides to leave him. Ted is now faced with the tasks of housekeeping and taking care of himself and their young son Billy.

movies.title: Patton
movies.overview: "Patton" tells the tale of General George S. Patton, famous tank commander of World War II. The film begins with patton's career in North Africa and progresses through the invasion of Germany and the fall of the Third Reich. Side plots also speak of Patton's numerous faults such his temper and habit towards insubordination.

movies.title: The Sting
movies.overview: Set in the 1930s this intricate caper deals with an ambitious small-time crook and a veteran con man who seek revenge on a vicious crime lord who murdered one of their gang.

movies.title: The French Connection
movies.overview: Tough narcotics detective 'Popeye' Doyle is in hot pursuit of a suave French drug dealer who may be the key to a huge heroin-smuggling operation.

movies.title: Freebie and the Bean
movies.overview: Two San Francisco detectives want to bring down a local hijacking boss. But they'll have to get to him before a hitman does.

movies.title: Harold and Maude
movies.overview: The young Harold lives in his own world of suicide-attempts and funeral visits to avoid the misery of his current family and home environment. Harold meets an 80-year-old woman named Maude who also lives in her own world yet one in which she is having the time of her life. When the two opposites meet they realize that their differences don’t matter and they become best friends and love each other.

movies.title: Two-Lane Blacktop
movies.overview: A driver and a mechanic travel around the United States hopping from drag strip to drag strip in a 1955 Chevy Bel-Air coupe. They race for money, betting with their competitors. The pair gain a young and talkative female stowaway. Along the way they unintentionally attract a well-to-do drifter driving a new Pontiac GTO. This older man, looking for attention, antagonizes their efforts.

movies.title: Willy Wonka & the Chocolate Factory
movies.overview: Eccentric candy man Willy Wonka prompts a worldwide frenzy when he announces that golden tickets hidden inside five of his delicious candy bars will admit their lucky holders into his top-secret confectionary. But does Wonka have an agenda hidden amid a world of Oompa Loompas and chocolate rivers?

content_list.description: The Exorcist is released, making audiences around the world sick and causing them to faint, creating a global hysteria. The first blockbuster is released: Jaws; meanwhile, auteur cinema grows with Martin Scorsese and other great directors. The '80s arrive with low-budget productions and era-defining comedies.
